name: The example
why: 'two teams': your answer was checked. For example (True, [0, 1, 0, 1, 0]): every edge joins a 0 to a 1.

name: A triangle
why: 'odd cycle': (False, [0, 1, 2]) in any order round the triangle. Going round, the teams must change 3 times and end where they started: impossible.

name: No edges
why: 'two teams': any split works, for example [0, 0, 0].

name: Two parts
why: 'odd cycle': [3, 4, 5]. The part with 0 splits into two teams, but the triangle in the other part does not. Start a search from every vertex not yet given a team.

name: An edge given twice
why: 'two teams': [0, 1, 0]. A repeated edge is not a cycle of odd length.

name: The odd cycle is far away
show: a path 0–…–8, then a square 8–9–10–11 with a cross edge 9–11
why: 'odd cycle': [9, 10, 11] or [8, 9, 11]. The answer must be a real cycle: only the vertices where the two routes meet, not the path that led there.

name: A ring of 100,001
why: 'odd cycle': the whole ring. A recursive search goes about 100,000 calls deep and fails. A breadth-first search finds the clash halfway round; walk back from both ends to where the two routes meet (lesson 6).

name: A path of 100,000
why: 'two teams': even and odd places. Again too deep for recursion.

name: 170,000 edges across
show: 100,000 vertices; every edge joins an even vertex to an odd one
why: 'two teams'. The graph is one big part, and your teams are checked edge by edge.

name: One edge spoils it
show: the graph above, plus one edge between two even vertices
why: 'odd cycle'. One edge inside a team makes an odd cycle through it. The check follows your cycle edge by edge.
